question: Three colleagues divide a customer research report between them. Each works on their own section in their own separate chat, and the sections are combined the day before the deadline. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) Each section will be about the same length, giving the combined report an unhelpfully even balance across topics.
B) The three colleagues will each spend longer on their section than they would have spent working all together.
C) The sections will rest on different assumptions and definitions, and the combined report will not hold together.
D) The finished report will contain three different writing styles, which readers will notice as they move through it.
correct_answers: C) The sections will rest on different assumptions and definitions, and the combined report will not hold together.
explanations: Even section lengths are a cosmetic outcome, and easily adjusted once the material is in front of them.
Splitting the work reduces individual effort rather than increasing it, and effort is not what fails here.

Correct. Nothing is shared between the three chats, so each section quietly settles its own time period, customer segment definition and success measure. Those conflicts only surface at the merge, when there is a day left to resolve them.
Inconsistent voice is real and worth an editing pass, but it is visible on the surface and does not undermine the report's conclusions.
